intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is caused by homozygous mutation in the WNT10B gene (601906) on chromosome 12q13.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is caused by homozygous mutation in the WNT10B gene.
checks.evidence_quote: a homozygous missense WNT10b mutation (p.R332W) in all affected individuals but the atypical case plus in an asymptomatic female
checks.explanation: Homozygous WNT10B mutation found in autosomal recessive SHFM; SHFM6 designation is nomenclature.

checks.claim: The WNT10B gene is located on chromosome 12q13.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified by homozygosity mapping a novel SHFM locus at 12q13.11-q13 with a maximum multipoint lod score of 5.47 and by subsequent candidate gene approach a homozygous missense WNT10b mutation
checks.explanation: WNT10B identified as candidate within the 12q13 locus.

paragraphs.text: Split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM) is a limb malformation with central reductions of the hands and/or feet. Elliott and Evans (2006) noted that it is genetically heterogeneous, shows variable expressivity and reduced penetrance, and can occur in isolation, in syndromes, or with other distal limb anomalies such as polydactyly and/or syndactyly. Most familial cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner (Gül and Oktenli, 2002). SHFM6 is a form of the malformation that shows autosomal recessive inheritance (Ugur and Tolun, 2008; Blattner et al., 2010).

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM) is a limb malformation involving central reductions of the hands and/or feet.
checks.evidence_quote: Split hand and foot malformation syndrome (SHFM) is characterized by the absence of the central digital rays, deep median cleft, and syndactyly of the remaining digits.
checks.explanation: Absence of the central digital rays of the hands and feet amounts to central reduction. The paper also mentions a median cleft and syndactyly.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation is genetically heterogeneous.
checks.evidence_quote: genetic heterogeneity, with at least five loci identified to date, further complicates management of affected patients and their families.
checks.explanation: The abstract states directly that SHFM is genetically heterogeneous.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation shows variable expressivity and reduced penetrance.
checks.evidence_quote: SHFM can occur as an isolated malformation or in association with other malformations, as in the ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting (EEC) syndrome and other autosomal dominant conditions with long bone involvement, all showing variable expressivity and reduced penetrance.
checks.explanation: The abstract states variable expressivity and reduced penetrance.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation can occur in isolation, as part of syndromes, or with other distal limb anomalies such as polydactyly and/or syndactyly.
checks.evidence_quote: The deficiency in SHFM patients can also be accompanied by other distal limb anomalies including polydactyly and/or syndactyly.
checks.explanation: The abstract also says SHFM can be isolated or part of syndromes such as EEC, as quoted in the previous claim.

checks.claim: Most familial cases of split-hand/foot malformation are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
checks.evidence_quote: The majority of the familial cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

checks.claim: SHFM6 is a form of split-hand/foot malformation with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: We studied a large consanguineous kindred afflicted with autosomal recessive SHFM.

paragraphs.text: Kantaputra et al. (2018) reported an Indian girl with split-hand/foot malformation, sparse hair, and interrupted eyebrows. The patient and all her family members had normal bone density and were not obese, unlike some patients with WNT10B variants. The authors suggested that sparse hair and interrupted eyebrows may be associated findings of SHFM6.

paragraphs.text: Freire-Maia (1971) described a recessive form of ectrodactyly and discussed what it means for genetic counseling. Verma et al. (1976) found affected individuals in 2 sibships of a consanguineous family, each born to first-cousin parents. They concluded that their report, together with earlier reports including that of Freire-Maia (1971), further showed that split-hand and split-foot deformity can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora and Nubani (1989) discussed the possibility of a rare autosomal recessive form of split hand/foot malformation. As an alternative, they proposed a 2-locus model. In this model, a gene at another locus controls the dominant mutation that causes split hand/foot malformation, and a dominant mutation at the controlling locus causes nonpenetrance of the split hand/foot mutation.

paragraphs.text: Ugur and Tolun (2008) and Blattner et al. (2010) found homozygous WNT10B mutations in patients with SHFM. In the family reported by Blattner et al. (2010), 9 heterozygous relatives were unaffected. Blattner et al. (2010) concluded that sporadic SHFM is not always a dominant trait and may be recessively inherited. In that case the recurrence risk is 25% for sibs and very low for offspring of patients, unless there is consanguinity.

paragraphs.text: Ugur and Tolun (2008) used a candidate gene approach in a large consanguineous kindred with autosomal recessive SHFM and found a homozygous missense mutation in the WNT10B gene (R332W). The mutation was present in all affected members except the one with an atypical phenotype, and it was also present in 1 asymptomatic female. The authors proposed 2 explanations: either a second locus contributes to the SHFM phenotype, or a suppressor locus prevented the phenotype in the nonpenetrant female.

paragraphs.text: In an Indian girl with SHFM, sparse hair, and interrupted eyebrows, Kantaputra et al. (2018) found a homozygous 3-bp deletion in the WNT10B gene (c.695_697delACA). The deletion was predicted to remove asn232 (N232del) without shifting the reading frame. Protein modeling suggested that removing this critical residue would severely affect protein structure and function, likely shortening the protein's lifetime and preventing it from binding its receptors and other ligands.

One affected member with the mildest, atypical phenotype did not carry it, and 1 asymptomatic female was homozygous for it.
